actSpeakBrief: Every prompt below needs a verdict, not a survey.
actSpeak1: Your town is closing its high street to cars next month. Argue for it to a shopkeeper who is against — and grant them their real losses first.
actSpeak2: Name one measure for an ageing population that would genuinely work, and say who would hate it and why.
actSpeak3: Now take a topic where you truly cannot decide, and force yourself to a verdict in sixty seconds.
actWriteBrief: More and more people work entirely from home. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Decide in the introduction, and make your last paragraph say why the balance falls that way.
actPlaceholder: Introduction: reframe the question, concede, then give your verdict…
coverSub: Two more essay types, two more band 9 answers taken apart — and the two ways a well-written essay still fails to answer the question
s2Title: Read the instruction, not the topic
s2A: "Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?" demands a verdict. Listing both sides and stopping is the single most common way this type is failed.
s2B: "What problems… and what measures?" demands two matched halves. Every measure must answer a problem you actually raised.
s2Note: Both band 6 answers in this lesson are competently written. Each one fails on the instruction above, and nothing else in them can make up for it.
s3Title: The question asks you to decide
s3A: "Outweigh" is a verb of comparison. An essay that presents two lists of equal weight has described a set of scales without reading them.
s3B: You may decide either way, or say the balance is close. What you cannot do is leave it to the reader to work out what you think.
s4Title: The verdict, in the second sentence
s4A: "Although…" concedes before it claims. One clause admits the other side exists, which stops the verdict sounding naive.
s4B: "Clearly outweigh" answers the question in the words it was asked in. No examiner has to interpret anything.
s5Title: Two gains, one of them slow
s5A: Two advantages, ranked and dated. One is immediate and one accrues over years — saying so is what turns a list into an argument. The last clause quietly kills the strongest objection shopkeepers make, without naming it yet.
s7A: Give the objection its best version, then answer it. The writer names three real people it would hurt — and then shows the objection argues for a better scheme rather than no scheme. A disadvantage you have disarmed weighs less; that is how the scales actually tip.
s8Title: Say why the balance falls that way
s8A: Broad and permanent against concentrated and fixable — four words that state the criterion the verdict was reached on.
s8B: The condition survives to the last line, so the essay ends as one argument rather than two halves and a summary.
s9A: It never decides. "Both sides have good arguments" is the sentence the question was written to prevent. Note also "more healthy" for healthier, and a conclusion that hands the decision to governments, when the question asked the writer to make it.
s11Title: Two halves that have to match
s11A: Two problems, well chosen, beat four listed. Each one needs enough space to show why it is a problem, not merely that it is one.
s11B: Every measure must answer a problem you raised. A solution to something you never mentioned reads as a second essay glued on.
s12Title: Name both halves before you start
s12A: "Financial and practical" tells the reader there are exactly two problems coming, and which order they arrive in.
s12B: The measures get a direction, not a preview. One clause sets the principle the solutions will share.
s13Title: The problems, one costed, one not
s13A: Each problem is explained by its mechanism, not asserted. Not "pensions are expensive" but the ratio that makes them so; not "people are lonely" but the specific labour that used to be free and no longer is. A problem the reader can see working is a problem a measure can be aimed at.
s15A: Measure one answers problem one; measure two answers both. The final clause says so out loud, which is the cheapest way to prove the halves are matched. Note also that the writer admits the first measure is unpopular — a measure presented as costless is one nobody has thought about.
s16Title: A conclusion with a thought in it
s16A: Two sentences are enough. Nothing new is argued; the frame the essay used is simply named.
s16B: Compare it with "if we all work together we can solve it" — the same length, and no content whatever.
s17A: The measures do not answer the problems. The problem was that pensions cost more than the state can raise; the first measure is to spend more, the second is a matter of manners, and the third solves a problem the essay never raised.
s19Ctx: Click an instruction on the left, then what it obliges you to produce.
x07a: Two ideas of equal weight is exactly what a list is. Ranking them is the difference between reporting the arguments and using them.
x07b: A reader can only weigh things that have been given weights. This is where an outweigh essay is won.
x07c: Neither is presented as doubtful. Both are asserted; what varies is how quickly each one arrives.
x07d: Length has no bearing. A ranked pair in one sentence would do the same work as this paragraph does.
x07e: In an outweigh essay, unranked advantages cannot outweigh anything.
x11a: More arguments make a longer list. The problem is not that the list is short — it is that nothing weighs it.
x11b: Range helps lexical resource, a quarter of the mark. It cannot repair an answer that has not addressed the task.
x11c: Task response asks whether the question was answered. This one was not — the verdict the question demands is simply absent.
x11d: It has examples of a kind. What it lacks is any statement of which side those examples add up to.
x11e: A missing verdict caps an outweigh essay however well the rest is written.
x15a: There is no rule about how many problems an essay may raise. Two is better here for what it makes room for, not because more is forbidden.
x15b: This answer is comfortably over the minimum either way. Cutting the count is not about saving words.
x15c: Development is marked, breadth is not. Two problems explained beat five named every time.
x15d: Any of the five would be relevant. Relevance is not what limits the number — space to develop them is.
x15e: Coverage is not the test. An underdeveloped point scores as if it were not there.
x19a: Governments are a perfectly good agent for a measure. The trouble is what this one is asked to do.
x19b: It is on topic. Being about the right subject is not the same as answering the problem raised about it.
x19c: Popularity is not the test — the band 9 answer proposes a deeply unpopular measure and scores for it.
x19d: The stated problem was a shortage of money. Answering it with more spending restates the problem as though it were the cure.
x19e: Read your measures back against your problems. If one restates the problem, it is not a measure.
x20a: Five of these six get written as though they were the same essay. They are not.
x21a: Outweigh — the question's own verb. Answering in the words you were asked in leaves nothing to interpret.
x21b: Unevenly — it names how the disadvantage works. A cost that is real but narrow can then be weighed against a gain that is broad.
x22a: Measure — the task's own noun. “Solution” works too, but echoing the paper costs nothing and proves you read it.
x22b: Addresses — the sentence that ties a measure back to the problem it answers. Without one of these, the two halves never visibly meet.
